transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?
I feel like I have to keep doing the same checks and routines over and over to make sure my wife is safe, and it’s taking up my whole day. I'm just so exhausted, and I don't know how to stop.
Can you tell me more about these checks and routines, what specifically do you feel compelled to do over and over to ensure your wife's safety?

I'm stuck in these exhausting routines, like reading her medication labels out loud, counting each pill three times, and checking the stove knobs and door locks in a precise order. I even find myself silently repeating a little phrase for good luck to make sure I've done it right. If I don't do these things exactly perfectly, I'm terrified I'll miss some tiny detail and something terrible will happen to her.
Do you feel that these repetitive thoughts and actions are unreasonable or excessive, or do they seem completely logical and necessary to you at the time you're doing them?

At the moment I'm doing them, they feel absolutely necessary and logical because the fear of something terrible happening to my wife is just so overwhelming. But intellectually, when I step back, I know these routines are completely irrational and excessive, though I still feel powerless to stop them.
Do you experience any intrusive thoughts or images that disturb you, such as fearing harm to your wife, in addition to the compulsions to perform these specific rituals?

Yes, I constantly get these relentless thoughts, like worrying I miscounted her pills and she'll stop breathing, or that a single crumb of salt on her plate will send her back to the hospital. The image of her dying because I overlooked something just replays in my mind over and over until I feel physically sick to my stomach.
How have these obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors affected your relationship with your wife and your ability to engage in work or other activities you enjoy?

It’s been devastating, and I just feel so incredibly exhausted and sad. I’ve had to almost entirely stop the volunteer literacy tutoring I used to love, and even simple things like sitting to watch a show with my wife or going out to see friends feel impossible now. I'm just constantly being pulled away to recheck something, so we can't even enjoy each other's company anymore.
Do your obsessive thoughts primarily focus on fears of harming others, such as your wife, or do they also include fears of harm coming to yourself or other types of obsessive thoughts?

My fears are almost entirely focused on something terrible happening to my wife because of a mistake I might make. I don't really worry about harm coming to myself at all. The overwhelming dread is just that she will suffer or die, and that it will be entirely my fault.
Have you ever experienced any episodes where you felt an overwhelming urge to harm your wife, even though that goes against your actual wishes or values?

No, I have never had any urge or desire to harm my wife. My fear is the exact opposite—I am absolutely terrified of making a mistake or overlooking some tiny detail that might accidentally cause her harm.
Do you often feel guilty or responsible for things that are beyond your control, even when you know intellectually that it's not your fault?

Yes, I feel an overwhelming, exhausting sense of responsibility, believing that if anything goes wrong and she ends up back in the hospital, it will be entirely my fault. Even though I know intellectually that I cannot control everything and that my fears are irrational, the terrifying thought of overlooking a tiny detail and causing her harm still drives me to do these checking routines.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms align with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), characterized by recurrent, intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions) that the patient feels driven to perform in response to those thoughts. The patient's excessive concern for their wife's safety, the specific and repetitive checking rituals, and the acknowledgment of these behaviors as irrational but feeling compelled to perform them are all indicative of OCD.
